title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory experiment (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detectable unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. We provide the sealed design identifier (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02), execution accounting, an explicit reconciliation of runtime determinism (adapter enforcement vs model sampling parameters), the preregistered Mininet 10% holdout outcome (zero validator–emulator disagreements observed), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity.

sections.introduction: Automating the intent→configuration translation using large language models can materially reduce operator effort but risks producing incorrect or unsafe network changes (outages, policy violations). Prior work documents LLM factual errors and prompt sensitivity and proposes mitigation patterns that combine generation with deterministic validation and repair (generate–validate–repair, GVR) or other guardrails [1–4]. However, empirical, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of validator‑guided repair in operationally framed NetOps tasks are scarce. We therefore preregistered a narrow confirmatory question and executed an archived, auditable run: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The experiment used a paired shared‑initial design to isolate the effect of invoking the validator and the single permitted automated repair on the identical generator output. Our principal contribution is an artifact‑grounded, preregistered paired evaluation (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) and a concise operational interpretation of the observed null outcome.
sections.related_work: LLM hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism are documented across domains; proposed mitigations include grounding (RAG), verifier loops, and constrained agentic architectures [5–8]. In NetOps specifically, several prototypes and studies show feasibility of natural‑language intent translation to configurations and the utility of deterministic checkers (Batfish‑style) as policy/verifier components [2,9–11]. Red‑team and agent‑audit work highlights configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can change safety outcomes, motivating conservative validator and emulator checks [12–14]. Our study differs by preregistering a single preplanned confirmatory estimand, enforcing shared‑initial generation semantics to obtain a controlled paired contrast, and publishing complete execution accounting and statistical results so that the marginal effect of deterministic repair (under the tested constraints) can be directly assessed against prior proposals that argue for GVR as a general safety mechanism.
sections.methodology:
Preregistered design and estimand. The preregistration (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired binary design with n = 200 tasks. For each task the system produced one deterministic initial candidate that was reused for both conditions: (A) baseline (LLM‑only), where the initial candidate is checked by the primary deterministic validator and recorded; (B) guarded (GVR), where the same initial candidate is validated and—if the validator reports violations—one automated repair prompt is permitted and the repaired candidate is re‑validated. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the preregistered confirmatory test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were computed via bootstrap percentile with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Planned maximum model calls = 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); adapter enforcement limited actual calls per the execution contract.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks evenly distributed across four topology clusters: enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge). Tasks encode initial and expected final state plus declarative workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group‑active minima) that the deterministic validator enforces. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performs syntactic parsing and intent/constraint validation and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout to detect potential validator blind spots at the data plane.

Adapter semantics and runtime determinism. The experiment enforced a shared‑initial generation semantics implemented by the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter: each task produced a single initial LLM candidate that was reused across baseline and guarded conditions. The execution accounting shows hosted model call events = 200 and a single shared_initial_generation stage per task, confirming the single shared invocation per task; this adapter enforcement is the operational mechanism that produced determinism for the paired contrast. Model configuration metadata records the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and does not expose a runtime temperature scalar in a manner that would imply independent stochastic sampling; determinism for the confirmatory contrast therefore derives from adapter enforcement rather than relying on a model‑side temperature value. We make this explicit because a superficial reading of model metadata can conflate a null temperature field with nondeterministic sampling; here, determinism is adapter‑enforced and verifiable in the reconciliation/accounting artifacts.

Repair policy, randomization, and reproducibility parameters. The preregistered repair budget allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task. Task ordering was randomized with a fixed schedule recorded in the task manifest metadata. Bootstrap resampling used seed = 1729 with 10,000 resamples for paired CI construction. The Mininet holdout was drawn at random per the preregistration; however, a labeled artifact that explicitly records the RNG seed used to select the 10% holdout is absent from the archive. We therefore disclose that exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the holdout selection is not possible from the labeled artifacts; the contamination summary for the executed holdout nevertheless reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. All other handling rules (missingness, exclusions, contamination treatment) were preregistered and applied deterministically.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes. Summary: planned tasks = 200; completed pairs = 200; model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls used = 0 (no repair prompts issued). Adapter accounting confirms a single shared_initial_generation per task and zero failed model calls. There were no infrastructure execution failures or unscorable episodes.

Validator outcomes and primary analysis. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0). The paired 2×2 table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Under the preregistered estimand the observed paired difference = 0.0. The exact two‑sided McNemar test (preplanned) yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because there are no discordant pairs, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not evaluable on this sample: the baseline validator‑detectable unsafe incidence is 0% by construction of the observed outcomes.

Mininet holdout and contamination check. The preregistered Mininet-based disagreement detector was applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) and produced zero validator–emulator disagreement flags in the executed holdout. We reiterate the reproducibility caveat: the explicit RNG seed labeling the holdout selection is not present in the archived labeled artifacts, which prevents exact reconstruction of which tasks comprised the holdout despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.

Secondary outcomes. Because no validator failures occurred, the repair branch was never invoked and secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per repair) have no empirical observations in this run. Representative per‑task validator diagnostics confirm that parsed_command_count matched required_command_count and that validator validation_after.valid = true for sample tasks with declared difficulty labels such as medium/hard/very_hard, showing the task bank exercised nontrivial workflow constraints even though outputs were validator‑satisfying under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The observed null—no validator‑detected failures under the shared‑initial deterministic generation policy—is an artifact‑grounded factual outcome. It does not imply that GVR is generally ineffective; rather, it shows that the marginal utility of automated repair (with the constrained repair budget and the single shared candidate per task) is a function of baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage for the chosen workload and generation policy. When baseline validator failures are rare, a single‑round GVR with no resampling yields no measurable marginal benefit for validator‑detectable errors.

Why the null occurred (diagnostics). Three artifact‑grounded factors explain the null: (1) the generator+prompt policy produced initial candidates that satisfied the explicit machine‑checkable constraints encoded in the task bank (validator traces show parsed_command_count ≈ required_command_count and violation_count = 0); (2) the shared‑initial paired design intentionally removed sampling variance that might otherwise expose failing alternative draws; (3) the holdout Mininet checks (20 tasks) revealed no disagreements, although the absence of a labeled holdout RNG seed limits exact reconstruction of that check.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational implications. The shared‑initial paired design delivers a controlled internal estimate of the incremental effect of validation+repair on an identical output but excludes gains obtainable by re‑sampling the LLM (diverse draws) or by using multi‑step repair budgets. Practitioners should therefore measure two complementary quantities before deploying GVR: (A) the unconditional baseline failure prevalence under the intended generation policy (multi‑sample per task, nonzero temperature where applicable) and (B) validator completeness via emulation, vendor models, or testbeds. If baseline failures are low under the production policy, investing in broader validator coverage, adversarial testing, or sampling/ensemble policies may yield higher risk reduction per resource dollar than a single‑round automated repair budget.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and deterministic reconciliation confirming accounting. Construct validity depends on validator expressiveness: validators codify a set of checks that may not capture all device‑level idiosyncrasies. External validity is limited by the single model (gpt‑5‑mini), the shared‑initial deterministic sampling policy, and the curated task bank. Conclusion validity: with zero discordant pairs the primary confirmatory test is uninformative about the preregistered 50% relative reduction, but the null outcome is precisely reported and artifact‑verifiable.

Practical recommendations. For workload where baseline validator failures are low, future confirmatory runs should (i) include independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws to estimate unconditional failure rates; (ii) enlarge repair budgets and allow multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair pathways; (iii) scale secondary emulation checks and record explicit RNG seeds for holdout draws to enable bit‑for‑bit reproducibility; and (iv) evaluate multiple models or ensembles to probe model‑dependent brittleness. The archived execution and reconciliation records provide a reproducible template for implementing these changes and for verifying accounting and statistical pipelines.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired study (n = 200) comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation. Both conditions produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding a paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent on our curated task bank under the chosen generation policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. The results are artifact‑grounded and illustrate a practical lesson: the marginal benefit of automated repair depends critically on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage. Future work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, broaden validator fidelity and emulation checks, and explore multi‑sample/multi‑step repair designs to better quantify operational gains.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure. This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Orchestration/frameworks: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 were used for generation and task provision; the primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The experiment enforced shared‑initial generation semantics (one deterministic initial candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded conditions) by adapter enforcement; execution accounting confirms hosted model call events = 200 and a single shared_initial_generation stage per task. Preregistration freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial semantics) was frozen prior to any model calls. Execution timestamps: start 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls allowed up to 200 but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human role: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and pre‑lock constraints; after the autonomy lock the study design decisions, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, and revisions were autonomous. Deviations/restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Reproducibility gap: the explicit RNG seed that selects the randomized 10% Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout selection even though the executed contamination check reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. Initial master prompt archive: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage: the deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntactic and intent constraints and may not capture device‑level idiosyncrasies or emergent failure modes detectable only by expanded emulation or real devices.
Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks, which prior audits show can bypass naive defenses.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.
Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies and human‑in‑the‑loop escalation were not exercised here.
